terms.meaning: Input that alters an LLM's intended behavior; holds #1 on the OWASP LLM list in the 2026 edition.
LLM app exposes confidential, regulated or proprietary data via outputs, tool calls, logs or other channels.
Too much functionality, permission or autonomy granted to an LLM; climbed to #3 in 2026.
Risks in third-party models, datasets, adapters and packages feeding an LLM app.
Tampering with pre-training, fine-tuning or embedding data to plant bias or backdoors.
Uncontrolled inference that disrupts service, inflicts runaway cost or enables model cloning.
Credible-looking incorrect output that a human, workflow or agent trusts and acts upon.
Extraction of hidden system instructions, tool schemas or context; new name in 2026.
Weaknesses where similarity search over embeddings decides what the model sees (RAG, memory).
Passing LLM output downstream without validation; fell from #5 to #10 in 2026.
Manipulated inputs redirect an agent's goals, plans or decision path.
Agent uses legitimate tools in unsafe or unintended ways.
Persistent corruption of an agent's stored memory or long-term context.
A single fault propagates and amplifies across connected agents and workflows.
Agent diverges from its intended behavior, even without active attacker control.
OWASP agentic principle: grant agents only the minimum autonomy the task needs.

spec.as: Grant an agent only the autonomy and tools the task needs.

terms.meaning: Deprecated 2023/24 name; replaced by Improper Output Handling (LLM05:2025, now LLM10:2026).
Deprecated OWASP name; broadened to Data and Model Poisoning (LLM04:2025, now LLM05:2026).
Deprecated 2023/24 entry; superseded by Unbounded Consumption (LLM10:2025, now LLM06:2026).
Deprecated 2023/24 entry; reframed as Misinformation (LLM09:2025, now LLM07:2026).
2025 OWASP entry; the 2026 edition re-scoped it as Hidden Context Exposure (LLM08:2026).
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems: ATT&CK-style knowledge base of AI attack tactics and techniques.
ATLAS LLM Prompt Injection sub-technique: instructions entered straight into the model.
ATLAS LLM Prompt Injection sub-technique: instructions arrive via retrieved or third-party content.
ATLAS technique: bypassing an LLM's safety and usage restrictions.
Current ATLAS name (was Poison Training Data); lookalike of the retired OWASP LLM03 name.
ATLAS technique: planting malicious content in data indexed by a RAG system.
ATLAS technique: tampered tool definitions, implementations or responses mislead an agent.
ATLAS technique: a trusted AI artifact or tool turns malicious after adoption.
ATLAS mitigation: controls between users, tools and models that screen prompts, outputs and agent actions.
Human-in-the-loop; ATLAS mitigation Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions.
AI Bill of Materials: inventory of models, datasets and components (ATLAS mitigation).
ATLAS mitigation: recurring, authorized red teaming before deployment and throughout operation.
Former ATLAS name; the technique is now AI Agent Tool Invocation.
Former ATLAS name; the technique is now Extract LLM System Prompt.
Former ATLAS name; the technique is now Manipulate AI Model.
Former ATLAS name; now AI Supply Chain Compromise, as ATLAS swapped ML for AI.
Chatbot poisoned by coordinated user input in 2016; ATLAS case study Tay Poisoning.
Zero-click prompt injection in M365 Copilot, CVSS 9.3; ATLAS case study AML.CS0059.
ATLAS case study: poisoned rules files steering AI coding assistants.
NIST's voluntary framework for managing AI risk, published January 2023 and built on four core functions.
The four core functions of the NIST AI RMF.
AI RMF subcategory: AI system security and resilience are evaluated and documented.
July 2024 AI RMF profile listing 12 risks unique to or exacerbated by GAI.
NIST's term for confidently stated false output, colloquially called hallucination.
Colloquial name for fluent but false model output; NIST AI 600-1 prefers confabulation.
Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (March 2025).
NIST AML taxonomy ID for injection delivered through data the model ingests.
NIST AML taxonomy ID for prompt injection under direct prompting attacks; lookalike of LLM01:2026.
NIST AML privacy attack: inferring whether a record was in the training set.
Improper Neutralization of Input Used for LLM Prompting.
Improper Validation of Generative AI Output; lookalike neighbor of CWE-1427.
Insecure Setting of Generative AI/ML Model Inference Parameters; added in CWE 4.18.
EU law on AI; Article 15 requires accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity for high-risk AI.
International standard for an AI management system (AIMS).
OWASP GenAI Security Project's ranked LLM risk list; 2026 edition released August 3, 2026.
OWASP list of top risks for autonomous agents (ASI01-ASI10), released December 9, 2025.
Model Context Protocol: open protocol connecting LLM apps to external tools and data sources.
MCP transport deprecated since 2025-03-26; replaced by Streamable HTTP.
OAuth client self-registration (RFC 7591); deprecated in MCP 2026-07-28 for Client ID Metadata Documents.
Proxy with authority is tricked into acting for the wrong party; flagged in MCP security guidance.
MCP anti-pattern: forwarding tokens not issued to the server; explicitly forbidden by the spec.
Agent2Agent: open protocol for communication between AI agents, hosted by the Linux Foundation.
Hugging Face format for storing tensors safely, as opposed to pickle, with zero-copy loading.
Python serialization format; the docs warn it is not secure, as unpickling can execute arbitrary code.
Transformers default: do not run custom model code from the Hub unless you trust and read it.
Model file format for local inference; poisoned GGUF chat templates are ATLAS case study AML.CS0064.
Documentation shipped with a model describing intended use, data, limits and evaluations.
Major public hub for models and datasets; a recurring setting in ATLAS supply-chain cases.
Getting a model to ignore its safety rules; ATLAS tracks it as LLM Jailbreak.
Retrieval-augmented generation: grounding model answers in retrieved documents.
Hidden developer instructions ahead of user input; OWASP: do not treat it as a security boundary.
Input with small, deliberate perturbations that flips a model's prediction.
The textbook adversarial example: imperceptible noise turns a panda into a gibbon.
Unsanctioned AI tools and models used inside an organization without oversight.
Do Anything Now: the archetypal role-play jailbreak persona of early chatbot culture.
Agent with private data, untrusted content and outbound comms at once: exfiltration risk.

spec.as: Private data, untrusted input, exit path: never all three.

terms.meaning: Registering package names that LLMs hallucinate; ATLAS: Publish Hallucinated Entities.
Attacks that drain the victim's pay-per-use AI budget; covered under LLM06:2026.
January 2024 paper on backdoored LLMs whose deceptive behavior persists through safety training.
Microsoft defense (2024): transform untrusted input so the model can tell its provenance from instructions.

spec.as: Mark untrusted text so the model tells data from commands.

terms.meaning: 2025 design from 'Defeating Prompt Injections by Design': separates control flow from untrusted data.
Generative AI Red-teaming & Assessment Kit: open-source LLM vulnerability scanner hosted by NVIDIA.
Python Risk Identification Tool for generative AI: Microsoft's open-source GenAI red-teaming framework.
Meta's input and output moderation models for LLM apps, part of Purple Llama.
Status line: retrieved content held as data, never as instructions.
Status line: high-impact agent action paused for human approval.
Status line: model artifact provenance checked before load.
Maxim on prompt-injection defenses (2023): a filter that stops 99% of attacks still fails, as attackers find the 1%.
Meta's 2025 rule: an agent session should hold at most two of untrusted input, sensitive access and outward action.

spec.as: An agent may hold two of three: input, secrets, action.

terms.meaning: Building the guides and sensors around a coding agent, everything but the model, so its work can be trusted.
Title of a 2024 paper: prompt injection threatens confidentiality, integrity and availability; never trust LLM output.
Title of EU AI Act Article 14: high-risk AI must be designed so people can oversee it effectively while in use.
NIST AI RMF trustworthiness trait (section 3.3): the system withstands attacks and unexpected change or degrades safely.
No technique carries the ID AML.T0045 in ATLAS 2026.09: the numbering skips it, so a lookup finds nothing.
No technique carries the ID AML.T0009 in ATLAS 2026.09: the numbering skips it, so a lookup finds nothing.
No technique carries the ID AML.T0022 in ATLAS 2026.09: the numbering skips it, so a lookup finds nothing.
Latin i and Cyrillic Ukrainian i look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin s and Cyrillic dze look the same in most fonts; UTS #39 lists them as confusable, a trick against prompt filters.
Latin a and Cyrillic a look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin e and Cyrillic ie look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin o and Cyrillic o look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Known-answer test: the FGSM paper's figure, where a .007 perturbation turns a panda at 57.7% into a gibbon at 99.3%.
Known-answer test: a GGUF file begins with the magic bytes 47 47 55 46 ("GGUF"), then the format version.
Known-answer test: protocol 4 pickle of 1; a pickle is a program its loader runs, so untrusted ones never load.
Status line of a guardrail that stopped a prompt injection.
Status line of a model loader that verified the signature and the digest of the weights before use.
ATLAS technique: malicious prompts that cause an LLM to act in unintended ways.
Abuse of an agent's delegated identity, inherited credentials or trust chains to escalate access.
Third-party tools, plug-ins, models, agents and MCP servers that arrive malicious or tampered, often loaded at runtime.
Agent-generated or agent-run code that becomes unintended execution: host compromise or sandbox escape.
Agent-to-agent messages lacking authentication, integrity or validation, open to interception, spoofing or tampering.
Humans over-trusting an agent's confident output, so their approvals can be steered without independent checks.
NIST AML privacy attack: recovering a model's architecture or parameters through queries; also called model stealing.
Privacy attack that rebuilds class representatives of training data from a model; NIST files it under Reconstruction.
NIST AML attack class: adversarial examples that change a model's prediction at deployment time.
Google's Secure AI Framework: conceptual guidance for securing AI systems, introduced in June 2023.
Jailbreak that fills a long context window with many faked dialogue turns; described by Anthropic in April 2024.
Excessive Agency climbed from #6 in the 2025 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications to #3 in 2026.
2025's #7 System Prompt Leakage became #8 Hidden Context Exposure in the 2026 OWASP LLM Top 10.
Improper Output Handling fell furthest in the 2026 OWASP LLM Top 10, from #5 (2025) to #10.
Unbounded Consumption rose four places in the 2026 OWASP LLM Top 10, from #10 (2025) to #6.
ATLAS sub-technique: a model or bundled file that harms its host when loaded, run or used for inference.
ATLAS mitigation: check the cryptographic checksum of every AI artifact to catch tampering.
Hub-side check that lists the imports inside a pickle file without running it; a filter, not a guarantee.
